Yaqui

Yaqui or Yoeme people have homelands in Sonora’s Yaqui River valley and continuing communities across the modern U.S.–Mexico border. This guide begins with the Texas Band’s own account and keeps it distinct from Pascua Yaqui institutions in Arizona and the Sonora-focused works.

Two newly inspected scholarly works broaden the six-work foundation with selected Sonora environmental history and attributed Pótam oral-history research. Eight substantive works do not yet provide balanced Texas migration history or comprehensive Sonora coverage. Existing supporting references and unread leads remain excluded; selected excerpt review is explicit.

Assessment recorded October 26, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

  • Independent Texas migration records and fuller Sonora community-directed historical publications remain needed; the new scholarly works do not corroborate the Texas Band’s specific Presidio/Fort Davis narrative.
  • The 2017 environmental-history article was inspected only in the selected pages; its underlying archives were not inspected. Current land and water questions remain outside this bounded review.
  • The 2023 oral-history study concerns two women in Pótam and the researcher’s interpretations. It is not a survey or community endorsement.
  • The earlier 1936 book and 2016 dictionary remain selected-excerpt reviews; existing legal-status uncertainties and the unavailable INPI route remain open.
  • No community review or endorsement is recorded.

01

A Texas community account

The Texas Band of Yaqui Indians describes its community through Yoeme family histories of displacement from Sonora and continuing relationships with Yaqui pueblos there. Its longer institutional account places a Presidio/Fort Davis connection in the 1870s. These details are attributed to this publisher; the underlying family and archival records were not inspected. The two pages form one institutional account, not two independent historical confirmations.

Read the sources [4] Texas Band of Yaqui Indians [5] Texas Band of Yaqui Indians

02

Read the 2015 Texas resolution directly

Texas Senate Resolution 989 was adopted on May 27, 2015. Its operative clauses honor the Band’s members and request a commemorative copy. The historical recitals should be read alongside the community account rather than treated as an independent archival investigation. This review does not determine broader legal effects or equate the resolution with federal acknowledgment.

Read the sources [6] Texas Senate [4] Texas Band of Yaqui Indians

03

Keep the Arizona statute in its own scope

Public Law 95-375, enacted September 18, 1978, addresses the named Pascua Yaqui association and Tribe in Arizona. It provides for federal-service eligibility and includes trust-land, governing-document and membership provisions. This is an historical enactment, not a statement of every Yaqui community’s status or of current membership rules. Later amendments were not reviewed.

Read the sources [9] United States Congress

04

Language teaching and individual experience

The Pascua Yaqui Teacher Language Institute describes goals for preparing language instructors, curriculum and family language use. These are stated educational aims, not measured outcomes. On the same page, instructor Graciela Garcia describes growing up with Yaqui as a first language and facing difficulties learning English at school. Her account is an individual experience, not a generalization about all Yaqui speakers or Texas education.

Read the sources [10] Pascua Yaqui Tribe

05

A dictionary shaped with Yaqui educators

The 2016 Diccionario yaqui de bolsillo presents Yaqui–Spanish and Spanish–Yaqui material. Its acknowledgments credit Yaqui-speaking teachers, and its teacher-written foreword explains educational and intergenerational purposes. The inspected front matter supports that collaborative context; it does not establish present fluency, universal dialect coverage or a full review of the entries.

Read the sources [12] Crescencio Buitimea Valenzuela, Zarina Estrada Fernández, Aarón Grageda Bustamante, Manuel Carlos Silva Encinas; Universidad de Sonora

06

A community reading route

The Pascua Yaqui Tribal Library describes Hiaki special collections, literacy support and family programming. Its page links readers to books, catalogues and digital services. The library account is useful educational context; each linked book still needs its own review. Availability and account requirements of the individual services were not checked.

Read the sources [11] Pascua Yaqui Tribe

07

Reading a 1930s research encounter

In the selected introduction to the 1936 Texas Technological College study, Holden describes how intermediaries and translation shaped the expedition’s access to Sonora communities in 1934. This helps readers examine who recorded an account and how. The excerpt is not direct evidence of Texas settlement. The later chapters and illustrations were not reviewed, and hosting by a present-day Tribal library is not blanket endorsement.

Read the sources [8] W. C. Holden and colleagues; Texas Technological College

08

Scope and the next reading steps

This is a foundational source guide, not an adequate wider Yaqui history. The selected river-history and Pótam oral-history works add Sonora perspectives but do not settle the Texas migration account. Continue with community-directed history, documented migration records and language scholarship. The museum sheet is brief orientation; the retained INPI route remains unread. Follow cultural materials through the relevant community publisher and stated scope.

Read the sources [4] Texas Band of Yaqui Indians [7] Arizona State Museum, University of Arizona [12] Crescencio Buitimea Valenzuela, Zarina Estrada Fernández, Aarón Grageda Bustamante, Manuel Carlos Silva Encinas; Universidad de Sonora [13] Esther Padilla Calderón; Culturales, Universidad Autónoma de Baja California [14] Edna Lucía García Rivera; Alteridades, Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana

09

A river landscape that changed over time

Historian Esther Padilla Calderón explains how the Yaqui River’s floods supported cultivation while sometimes damaging or relocating settlements. Her selected historical account describes a major channel change in 1833 and later attempts to control the river through irrigation works and dams. This helps readers see the Sonora homeland as a changing lived landscape. Her explanation combines archival material with earlier scholarship; the underlying archival files were not inspected for this guide. It does not establish present water allocations or Texas settlement history.

Read the sources [13] Esther Padilla Calderón; Culturales, Universidad Autónoma de Baja California

10

Listening to women’s memories in Pótam

Edna Lucía García Rivera’s 2023 study follows the memories of two older women living in Pótam. They recall ancestors’ displacement, survival and return, and connect those memories with responsibilities to family and community. García Rivera interprets their accounts through oral history and postcolonial feminist scholarship. These are named individual perspectives shaped by remembrance and the research encounter. They enrich the history without standing for every Yaqui woman or independently confirming each event recalled.

Read the sources [14] Edna Lucía García Rivera; Alteridades, Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana

What needs further research

  • Substantive Texas migration history still rests mainly on one institutional account; primary records and distinct community perspectives remain needed.
  • No comprehensive Sonora community-history, land/water-history or language review has been completed.
  • The 2015 resolution’s broader legal effects, the older About page’s reservation/treaty assertion and related certificates remain unassessed; no federal-status equivalence is inferred.
  • The 1936 book and 2016 dictionary were inspected only in the selected front matter/introduction, not in full.
  • Program descriptions establish stated activities/aims, not outcomes, speaker counts or universal practice.
  • The INPI original page remained unavailable to direct retrieval; indexed search text was not counted.
  • No community review or endorsement is recorded.
  • The new 2017 river-history work was read only in selected pages, and its underlying archival files were not inspected.
  • The 2023 Pótam study offers two women’s memories and a scholar’s interpretation, not a representative survey or independent verification of every recalled event.
  • The existing Sonora river photograph provides landscape context; a specifically relevant Texas Band picture remains a separate gap.

Los yaquis y las crecientes del río. Una historia del control hidráulico del río Yaqui — selected pages ↗

Padilla Calderón, Esther. 2017. Culturales 5(2): 67–106.

Publication: 2017-09-29

A historian’s analysis of changing relationships among river floods, cultivation and hydraulic infrastructure. The selected pages connect Yaqui settlement and farming with river change; this is a Sonora historical study, not Texas migration evidence. Its arguments and cited archival documents should be distinguished from directly inspected primary records.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Publisher record plus actual publisher PDF: printed pp. 67–69, 75–80 and 97–99 (PDF pages 1–3, 9–14 and 31–33 of 40). Title page visually inspected. Remaining narrative and bibliography were not content-reviewed; figure captions in selected text were read, but maps/figures were not visually evaluated or reused.

Review recorded: October 26, 2026
